deities: Samaleswari (Samalei Maa) - form of Durga/Shakti, worshipped as Jagatjanani, Adishakti, Mahalaxmi and Mahasaraswati
festivals: Nuakhai (regional harvest festival; first produce offered to the goddess)

history.summary: Maa Samaleswari, 'Samalei Maa', is the presiding goddess of Sambalpur and western Odisha; the city of Sambalpur is named after her. The present stone temple on the left bank of the Mahanadi in Sambalpur town is most widely attributed to King Balaram Dev (Balaram Singh), first Chauhan ruler of Sambalpur (r. c. 1540-1560), who is said to have built it after the goddess appeared in his dream asking for a temple on the riverbank; legend says the idol is a natural granite rock formation. The temple was rebuilt during the reign of King Chhatra Sai Deo (1657-1665). CONFLICT (verify): a travel-review source claims 'built in 1471 by Raja Baldev Singh', which predates the Chauhan dynasty's Sambalpur foundation - the 16th-century Balaram Dev attribution (also given by Wikipedia and regional histories) is the better-supported account. Kalinga-style architecture with rekha vimana; inner sanctum is cave-like. A separate four-armed-Durga Samaleswari temple at Sonepur (IGNCA report) is a different shrine, not this one.

name: Maa Samaleswari Temple
town_description: Sambalpur is the commercial and cultural capital of western Odisha, lying on the Mahanadi river about 320 km northwest of Bhubaneswar. It is famous for the Sambalpuri ikat textile tradition, the Hirakud Dam (one of the longest earthen dams in the world, ~15 km away), and its role in the freedom struggle led by Veer Surendra Sai. Sambalpur is named after Goddess Samaleswari, its presiding deity.

travel.airport: Veer Surendra Sai Airport, Jharsuguda ~35-40 km (limited flights); Biju Patnaik International Airport, Bhubaneswar ~320 km
travel.road: Temple is in the central city area on the Mahanadi bank; well connected by NH 53 and state buses

visitor_information.best_time: October-February; Nuakhai (August-September) is the biggest festival
visitor_information.opening_hours: An older source lists morning Mangal Aarti ~5 am, midday prasad ~noon with a short closure, evening aarti ~8 pm - (verify, 2010-era source)
